title: Chapter 60 – Counting Graves
html:
[Lin Clan – Lin Jian]

By the end of the first month, Jian has counted every grave on the hill, and he does not like the sum.

He does it on the first cold morning of autumn, in the pale light before the hill wakes, with a stick of charcoal and a roll of drawing paper on his knee. He has taken the upper path, the one that winds through the pines behind the ancestral hall, past the old stone stele and the three small shrines, to the long terraced slope where the Lin dead have been laid for four hundred years. There is a mist on the grass. The pine needles are wet and brown. His breath comes out in white curls.

He walks the rows. He writes as he goes.

Lin Shoucheng, the Founder. Eleven generations of Patriarchs, in a line along the crest. Wenhai, in a new mound, with a silver pencil case buried at its foot. The old Patriarch, his grandfather, under a tall gray slab with a name carved in a stern square hand, and a few dry flowers that his father has not let anyone clear away. Lin Mao, in the row below, with the earth still raw, a bunch of bitter yellow chrysanthemums and a small iron spear.

He stops at Mao's grave longer than the others. He does not know why. He stands with his hands in his sleeves, looking at the little spear stuck upright in the earth, and thinks of a short bald man with a steel-colored beard, saying, in the middle of a ruin, with a hook through his ribs: eleven breaths.

Twelve, he thinks. I told him twelve.

He writes the number. He moves on.

There are thirty-one new graves from the siege, in three long rows along the lower terrace. They are marked with plain wooden stakes, each with a name in black ink and a little twist of white cloth. The women have kept them swept. There is a tin cup of water at the head of each, and a few of them have a small toy, or a pebble, or a folded paper crane. He reads every name. He does not need to. He knows them. He knew every one.

Thirty-one, he writes.

He stops.

He looks at the number for a long time. Then he adds, in the margin, in a smaller hand, the others. Nine in the culvert. Mao, and four, at the Narrows. The old Patriarch. Wenhai. Two Red Ridge men, who died in the cellar, and were buried with the rest, because it is not a thing the Lin do, to leave a man out. He draws a line under it. He adds it.

Forty-nine.

It is a very small number, in a column. It is smaller than the roll of the dead at the Founder's Gate. It is a good deal smaller than what Mu would have done. But he stands on the wet slope, in the pale morning, with the charcoal black on his fingers, and he cannot make it say anything but what it says.

Fifty-one people, and I was the one who counted.

* * *

The clan has changed.

He sees it as he comes down the hill, in the long gold slant of the early sun. There is a smell of smoke and sawn timber on the wind. Along the great wall, where the western gate once hung, a dozen men are laying new stone. They are singing, quietly, one of the old road songs, in a ragged chorus. In the kitchen yard a long line of women are carrying baskets of grain from the store, and a boy in a patched jerkin is leading an ox to the trough. A hum of ordinary life goes up from every terrace. It is the sound of a place that is mending.

Nobody speaks to him as he passes. They look. They look at the small thin boy in the gray cloak, with a roll of paper under his arm, and then they look away, and he sees, in the corner of each averted face, a quick sidelong shyness, a kind of awed embarrassment, as of people who have been told a thing they do not know how to say.

They know.

It is not what he feared. He had thought it would be fear. It is something much odder and more difficult to bear: a respect so large and so shy that it will not look him in the face. He is, by common agreement, a ten-year-old boy who killed Mu. He is the one who found the Garden. He is a prodigy, a Seed-bearer, a five-element child, and the Mirror said so before the Arbiter of the Outer Court.

An old woman in a blue headcloth steps out of her doorway as he goes by, and presses something into his hand without a word. It is a small hot dumpling wrapped in a leaf. She is gone before he can thank her.

He eats it, sitting on a wall, in the sun. It is very good.

* * *

The announcement is made on the ninth day of the eighth month, in the great hall, at noon.

It is Wenyuan's idea. He has stood, in the long cold weeks since the siege, over a desk covered in ledgers, with the black circles under his eyes growing darker, and he has come, at last, to a decision. It is a hard one. It has cost him a good deal of sleep. When it is made, he calls the whole clan together, every man, woman and child, three hundred and ninety-one souls, in the broad low hall where eleven Patriarchs have sat, and stands before them on the dais, in a clean gray robe, with his hands behind his back.

"I have a thing to tell you," he says.

Nobody breathes.

"You know most of it. You have seen the seam. You have gone through it. You have sat on the moss of a garden under the hill, and drunk water out of a skin, and wondered what it was." The quiet, level, rather tired voice fills the hall without effort. "I will tell you what it is."

He tells them.

He tells it plainly. He does not dress it up. He tells them of the Orchard, and the Wardens, and the reservoir, and the lock plate that waits under it. He tells them of the vein, three parts in a hundred, and what has been drinking it. He tells them that the thing that has been killing the hill for four hundred years is the same thing that, if it is fed, will keep it. He tells them, in a plain dry voice, without looking at his son, how it was found. A boy of ten, a young seamwalker, a night in the quarry.

There is a long silence when he has finished.

Then, from the back of the hall, a thin creaky voice says: "And who is to have the herbs?"

It is the old schoolmaster. He is standing at the end of a row, very straight, in his patched gray gown, with his hands folded on his stick. His thin gray face is mild and attentive. He looks like a man who has asked a question in a lesson, and would like it answered properly.

"All of us," says Wenyuan.

"By what measure?"

"By need. First the sick, and the wounded. Then the children. Then the guards, who must keep it. Then the rest." He lifts his head. "It is not a treasure, Master Ji. It is a duty. It is also, I think, the only thing in four hundred years that has belonged to everybody."

The old man considers it. His thin lips move. After a long time he nods, once, with a small short bow, as a teacher acknowledges a correct answer.

"Then I have no further questions," he says.

* * *

It is Zhong who stands next.

He has been sitting at the end of the front row for the whole of the hearing, with his white head bowed and his heavy hands lying in his lap. He has not moved. He has not looked at anyone. He rises now, slowly, with a hand on the arm of the bench, and turns to face the hall.

He looks very old. He has lost thirty pounds in a month. The soft heavy face has fallen in on itself, and his white mustache hangs ragged and limp, and there are gray pouches under his eyes the color of ash. For a long moment he says nothing at all.

"I should like to speak," he says.

The Patriarch inclines his head.

"I sold the western gate." The voice is hoarse. It does not shake. "You all know it. The Arbiter read the letter. I will not tell you why. I have told the Patriarch, and I will tell you if you ask, but I do not think it matters." A long breath. "A man is not judged by his reasons. He is judged by what he did. And what I did is in the ground, on the lower terrace, in thirty-one rows."

Nobody speaks. In the third row, a woman in black has put a hand over her mouth.

"I have no right to ask for anything," says Zhong. "I ask nothing. I have given the three farms to the clan's common store, in trust, to be held until the last of the dead is mourned. I have given my house to the widows. I will live in the gatehouse, and keep the ledger of the Garden, if the Patriarch will have me. I will take no stipend. I will count." His mouth twists. "It is the only thing I was ever good for."

"Uncle," says Wenyuan, quietly.

"Do not." The old man's eyes close. "Do not be kind. I cannot bear it. I have been waiting a month for someone to strike me, and nobody has, and I think I should rather they did."

He stands in the silence, with his eyes shut, like a man at the end of a plank.

Then, from the front of the hall, there is a small sound. A woman has risen. She is thin and tired and dressed in white, and she carries a baby on her hip, and her young face is pale and set and quite steady.

It is Mao's daughter.

She walks the length of the aisle. She does not look to either side. She stops in front of Lin Zhong, close, a pace from his bowed white head, and looks at him for a long time. Then she lifts her free hand, and puts it, quite gently, against his cheek.

"My father counted," she says. "On the road. He counted eleven. The boy told me it was twelve." Her voice is very low. "I don't know which is true. But I know that he went because he was asked, and that he would have gone if you had not sold anything at all. He was that sort of man." A long pause. "I will not forgive you. I do not think I can. But I will not strike you either. You may keep the ledger."

She lowers her hand. She goes back down the aisle, with the baby sleeping on her shoulder, and sits.

Zhong stands very still. A single tear runs down the side of his nose and drops from the end of his mustache, and he does not wipe it.

* * *

He goes to the quarry that night, alone, with the roll of paper under his arm.

It is a clear, cold, still night, with a great white moon riding high over the pines, and the whole of the hill silvered and small. The quarry lies below him in its bowl of shadow. He walks down the east side, along the stepped terraces, past the long low spoil heaps and the empty guard-post, and comes, at the foot of the east wall, to the place where two mounds lie side by side in the moon.

They are small. They are not marked. A little way off, under a thorn bush, he had found a flat stone, and he had used it. It lies at the foot of the mounds, bare and gray, with two dates scratched on it in charcoal, and between them a single word.

Sisters.

He does not know whether they would have liked it. He has not told anyone. It is the one grave on the hill that is not on his list, and he is not sure it should be. But he has kept the promise, in the dark, with a spade, in the first week after the siege, with Pebble sitting on a rock to watch. He had burned them as Mei Lian asked, on pine, with a bit of slag for heat. He had waited all night for the ash to cool. And he had said, in the cold white dawn, to two small heaps of gray powder in a hole, a sentence he had spent days composing.

I am sorry. I did my best. It was not enough.

Now he sits on the ground in front of the stone, in the moon, with his knees drawn up and the paper unrolled on the grass beside him. He does not say anything. He has nothing to say. He only looks at the two small mounds, and at the word, and the cold bright moon on the thorn.

After a time there is a rustle in his collar.

Cold, says Pebble.

I know.

Not the cold of the night. The other cold. She is quiet for a moment. You are thinking of them again.

Yes.

They were bad.

They were. He puts a hand on her back. She has grown, in a month, perhaps an inch, and the bare places along her flanks have begun to show a faint pale fuzz, like the down on a chick. They were bad, and they were also sisters.

I do not understand.

I do not think anyone does. He looks at the stone. I think it is just a thing you carry.

She is silent. After a while she crawls out of his collar and down his arm and into his lap, and settles there, with her scaled tail round her nose, and her warm breath against his wrist.

I will carry it too, she says. If it is heavy.

Thank you.

It is not a favor, she says, with dignity. It is what one does with a friend.

* * *

Hu shows him the blade on the twentieth day.

It is a small thing, in the end. They have kept it, in the granary, in a chest lined with oilcloth, since Hu found it in the moss of the Orchard on the morning after, lying where Mu dropped it, in its black silk. It is a short narrow knife with no guard. The steel is the color of a dark river, with a faint wet shine, and along the spine, in Coral Gate script so fine that Jian cannot read it, a line of tiny characters runs from hilt to point. It is, Hu says, the finest thing he has ever seen made by a hand other than his own.

He holds it in his steady right hand. It does not shake. It has not shaken for twenty days.

"Pool-grade iron," he says. "Profound. Forged on a new moon, quenched in blood, as the book says. He made it perfectly. It was a real key." The old man turns the blade in the lamplight. "It would have fit. I have been looking at the plate, and at this, for three weeks, and I will tell you something that I did not tell your father. It would have fit. He had the lock and the key, and he had a boy to open it, if he had ever thought of asking. He needed only the courtesy."

"It would not have opened for him."

"No. It wants a gardener." Hu's mouth twists. "I have never in my life been so glad that a man was too proud to say please."

"What will you do with it?"

"Melt it, I think. I thought so, the first week." The one dark eye is very steady. "It is a murder weapon, boy. It is the product of eleven years of one man's hunger. It has a drop of the master's blood in the steel. It should be put in a crucible and let go."

"But?"

"But I cannot." He lays the blade down in its chest, with a soft sigh. "It is too good. It is the one honest thing he ever made. I have spent forty years being ashamed of what I did at the Forge, and I find that I cannot be ashamed of this. It is a perfect piece of work, made for a bad end, by a man who loved something too much. I think I shall hang it in the forge, over the door, and look at it every morning. A man should be reminded what he is capable of."

Jian does not answer. He is looking at the knife.

"There is another thing," says Hu, more quietly. "I have been reading the Canon, the first volume. I have read it a hundred times. And last night, for the first time in forty years, I found the end of it."

"The last page was blank."

"It was. It was blank because it was written in something that cannot be seen. I put it by the lamp, and it did nothing. I put it by the sun, and nothing. And then, last night, I laid the blade on it, and the page spoke." He draws the book from his cloak, thin, bone-bound, dark with the oil of his skin, and opens it at the last leaf. "Look."

It is a single line. It is in the same cramped hand as the rest, but fainter, and it has no ornament. The ink is the color of dried blood.

The door is not for the one who opens it. It is for the one who is let in.

"What does it mean?" says Jian.

"I do not know." Hu closes the book. "I think the man who wrote it did not either. I think he wrote it as a man leaves a note on a table, for whoever comes after." He looks up. "I think it means that your garden is not the end of anything, boy. I think it is only the porch."

* * *

He breaks through on the thirty-first night.

He has not meant to. He has been waiting, as the interface said, for thirty days, and has used every hour. He has walked the Orchard, and counted the Wardens, and sat at the reservoir's edge with his feet in the green, drinking the slow sweet Qi in small measured sips, like medicine. He has been careful. He has let the Seed eat its fifth. He has done nothing at all to push.

It comes, in the end, by itself.

He is sitting at the foot of the stele, in the pearl-gray light, with the half scroll open on his knees, reading the line he has read a hundred times. The Seed is hungry. For the first season it takes a fifth of all that the body gains. It is a toll, and a fair one. And the thought comes to him quite quietly, out of nowhere, as a bird comes down onto a branch: the toll has been paid.

He lifts his head.

He feels it. It is the Seed. It is the small round dark thing, no bigger than a grain of rice, that has sat in the center of his dantian for four months, eating, and growing, and saying nothing. It put out a shoot on the night of the red garden, thin and green and shy, and has said nothing since. It is full. It has taken what it needed. And as he watches, in the quiet of his own body, with a clear and total attention, the shoot swells at its tip, and trembles, and opens.

Bloom, he thinks.

The whole of him sings.

It is not like the other breakthroughs. It is not a flood or a climb. It is a waking, a long soft unfolding, like the first flower of a plant in the sun. The five lights in his dantian, wood and fire, earth and metal and water, lean toward the little green thing and feed it. It is a flower. It is a flower with five petals, one for each season he has not yet lived, green and gold and brown and white and blue, and where they meet, in the heart, a small bright mark forms, round and still and perfect, like a seal pressed into wax.

Qi Refining, ninth stage, says the interface, quite softly, in a line of white. Peak.

He laughs. It is a small, helpless, wondering sound. He is sitting on the moss, in the Garden, with his hands on a half scroll, and tears are running down his face, and he is, for the first time in two years, entirely and perfectly happy.

Peak, he thinks. Ten years old. QR9. It is the top of a mountain. There is only one more stage, and it is not a stage of the body but of the world, the long dark door of the Foundation, where a man puts down the habit of his flesh and takes up the habit of the sky. He is not there yet. He will not be for years. But he can see it now. It is a long way off, and very bright, like a lamp in a window at the end of a road.


Rebuilding, he reads. Recommended.

He wipes his eyes with the heel of his hand. He is not sad. He is, he finds, a little frightened, and very much alive.

Ninth stage, says Pebble, with satisfaction, from the moss. Very good. Now you are a big boy.

I am ten.

Yes, she says. It is the same thing.

* * *

The dawn is gray when he leaves the Garden.

He comes up through the old seam in the cellar, with Pebble on his shoulder and the paper under his arm. The hall is silent. The stairs are cold. In the passage outside his parents' room he stops, with his hand on the wall, and listens. Beyond the paper door there is the slow regular breathing of two people asleep. His father's. His mother's. It is a sound he has been listening to, in the dark, for four months, without knowing why.

He goes on. He climbs to the roof of the east wing, where he sat on the night of the siege, and lies down on the tiles with his hands behind his head and the cold stars fading above him. The whole of the hill lies below. A single lantern burns in the gatehouse. A thin gray smoke goes up from the kitchen chimney. Somewhere in the lower yard a cock crows, and another answers.

Fifty-one, he thinks.

It is a number. It is a weight. It is a thing that he will carry, with the rest, up whatever stair he is climbing, in the long grave years ahead. He does not think it will get lighter. He thinks, perhaps, that it will not have to. That a man may carry a great load, if he knows what it is, and does not look away.

And forty-one on the hill who are alive because of me, says the cold part of him, as it always does, with a small dry honesty. And three hundred and ninety-one who are not buried yet.

It is not a comfort. It is simply true.

He lies there until the sun is up. And when he rises, stiff and cold, and shakes the dew from his cloak, a messenger is standing in the kitchen yard below, a thin young man in the gray robe of the Outer Court, with a long white envelope in his hand, asking, in a breathless, nervous voice, for the Patriarch of Green Pine.
